name: Japonic
summary: Japanese and its relatives: the Ryukyuan languages of Okinawa and the southern islands, and Hachijō on a small island south of Tokyo. Japanese has a written record from the 8th century and some 125 million speakers. The Ryukyuan languages, which the Japanese state long called dialects, are separate languages that split from Japanese before its earliest texts, and all of them are now endangered.

sources.citation: Hammarström, Harald, Robert Forkel, Martin Haspelmath & Sebastian Bank. Glottolog: Japonic (japo1237).
Frellesvig, Bjarke. 2010. A History of the Japanese Language. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

essay.title: From 'Dialects' to a Family
essay.body:
For most of its history Japanese was treated as a language without relatives. The Ryukyuan languages changed that picture, but slowly, because the Japanese state and much of Japanese scholarship classed them as *hōgen*, 'dialects', of Japanese.

The first systematic demonstration came from **Basil Hall Chamberlain**, a British scholar teaching in Tokyo, whose *Essay in Aid of a Grammar and Dictionary of the Luchuan Language* (1895) set out regular correspondences between the speech of Shuri and Japanese. He showed that the two share basic vocabulary, verb morphology and grammatical particles, and that their differences are regular rather than random: Shuri *i* and *u* stand where Japanese has *e* and *o*, over and over again. The Okinawan scholar **Iha Fuyū** (1876–1947) then made the old Ryukyuan songbook, the *Omoro Sōshi*, a subject of philological study, giving the comparison a written time depth.

The harder step was to show that Ryukyuan is a sister of Japanese rather than an offshoot of it. In the 1950s **Hattori Shirō** argued, partly from lexicostatistics and partly from sound correspondences, that Ryukyuan separated from the ancestor of Japanese before the 8th-century texts. Later work found Ryukyuan distinctions, in vowels and in accent classes, that Old Japanese had already lost. A language cannot regain distinctions its ancestor had merged, so Ryukyuan must descend from an earlier stage.

Reconstruction followed: Maner Lawton Thorpe's Proto-Ryukyuan (1983), Samuel Martin's *The Japanese Language Through Time* (1987), and the Proto-Japonic work of John Whitman, Bjarke Frellesvig, Alexander Vovin and Thomas Pellard. The English name 'Japonic', which avoids calling the Ryukyuan languages 'Japanese', has since become standard. In 2009 UNESCO's atlas of endangered languages listed six Ryukyuan languages and Hachijō as separate languages.

essay.title: From Kyushu to the Islands
essay.body:
The Japonic family is young by the standards of Indo-European or Austronesian. Its common ancestor, Proto-Japonic, is usually placed in the first millennium BCE, and most scholars tie its arrival in Japan to the Yayoi culture: wet-rice farmers who crossed from the southern Korean peninsula to northern Kyushu. Radiocarbon dates published in the 2000s pushed the beginning of the Yayoi period back to around the 10th century BCE, although many archaeologists prefer a later date and the transition took centuries.

Three kinds of evidence support the link. Archaeologically, Yayoi rice paddies, tools and burials have close parallels in southern Korea. Genetically, mainland Japanese people descend from both the earlier Jōmon population and a later continental population, the 'dual structure' model proposed by Hanihara Kazurō in 1991 and since confirmed by ancient DNA. Linguistically, the internal diversity of Japonic is shallow: a Bayesian study of basic vocabulary by Sean Lee and Toshikazu Hasegawa (2011) dated Proto-Japonic to roughly 2,200 years ago, consistent with a Yayoi-period spread.

Before Japonic, the islands were home to the Jōmon peoples, whose languages are unknown. Ainu, in Hokkaido and formerly in northern Honshu, may be one survivor; others left no clear trace.

The move into the Ryukyus came much later. Archaeology shows farming communities arriving from Kyushu around the 10th–12th centuries CE, in the Gusuku period, and genetic studies point to substantial migration from the north, although dating it precisely is harder. This leaves a gap: the Ryukyuan languages split from Japanese before the 8th century, yet their speakers seem to have reached the islands only centuries later. The usual answer, argued by Thomas Pellard among others, is that pre-Ryukyuan was first a separate dialect in Kyushu. Where exactly it was spoken, and when it left, remain open.

essay.title: What the Languages Share
essay.body:
All Japonic languages are strongly head-final. The verb comes last, modifiers precede nouns, and grammatical relations are shown by particles placed after the noun: Japanese *Hanako ga hon o yonda* 'Hanako read a book' has *ga* marking the subject and *o* the object. There are no articles, no grammatical gender and no obligatory plural. Verbs and adjectives take chains of suffixes for tense, negation, politeness and mood, and adjectives inflect like verbs: Japanese *takai* 'is high', *takakatta* 'was high'. Speech levels and honorifics are built into the grammar.

The sound systems favour simple syllables of a consonant and a vowel, and timing is counted in morae rather than syllables: *Nippon* has four morae (*ni-p-po-n*). Most varieties have some form of pitch accent. In Tokyo Japanese *háshi* with a fall after the first mora means 'chopsticks' and *hashí* 'bridge'. Japonic also has *rendaku*, the voicing of the first consonant of the second part of a compound: *te* 'hand' plus *kami* 'paper' gives *tegami* 'letter'.

Some shared features are best seen historically. Old Japanese had *kakari-musubi*, in which a focus particle such as *zo* required the sentence to end in a special verb form. The construction had largely disappeared from Japanese by the 16th century but survives in Okinawan, where the focus particle *du* is its cognate, as in the saying *nuchi du takara* 'life is the treasure'.

Ryukyuan has innovations of its own: the raising of mid vowels, heavy palatalisation, glottalised consonants, and in Miyako syllables with no vowel at all.

For writing, Japonic has used Chinese characters from the start, along with the kana syllabaries developed from them. Okinawan court texts such as the *Omoro Sōshi* were written mainly in hiragana, and modern Ryukyuan writers use kana with extra conventions for sounds that Japanese lacks.

essay.title: Unsettled Questions
essay.body:
The deepest open question is whether Japonic has any relatives. The strongest candidate is Koreanic. Samuel Martin (1966) and John Whitman (1985) proposed sets of Japanese–Korean cognates, and the two languages are strikingly similar in grammar. Alexander Vovin, in *Koreo-Japonica* (2010), argued that most of the shared vocabulary is borrowing from a period when Japonic and Koreanic were in contact on the peninsula, and that the grammatical similarity is typological. A wider 'Transeurasian' family taking in Korean, Japanese, Tungusic, Mongolic and Turkic, defended by Martine Robbeets and colleagues (2021) with linguistic, archaeological and genetic data, is rejected by most historical linguists. Proposals linking Japonic to Austronesian or to Kra-Dai, notably Paul Benedict's 'Austro-Tai' (1990), have found little support. For now Japonic is usually treated as an independent family.

Closely tied to this is the question of Peninsular Japonic. Place names recorded in the Korean *Samguk sagi* (1145) for central Korea include apparent Japonic numerals and nouns. Christopher Beckwith (2004) took them as evidence that the Goguryeo language was Japonic; Vovin and Whitman read them instead as traces of Japonic spoken in the peninsula before Koreanic replaced it. Others doubt that the glosses can bear either interpretation.

Within the family, the reconstruction of Proto-Japonic is still debated. Old Japanese had eight vowels in its writing, but most scholars now reconstruct six for Proto-Japonic, with mid vowels *e* and *o* whose reconstruction rests partly on Ryukyuan evidence. How the Old Japanese 'second' vowels arose, and how many diphthongs to reconstruct, remain disputed.

Subgrouping is also contested at the edges. Some linguists see signs that the Ryukyuan languages share innovations with the dialects of southern Kyushu, which would mean that Ryukyuan is a sister of part of mainland Japonic rather than of the whole. The internal division of Ryukyuan into Northern and Southern branches is widely accepted, but the dating of each split is not.
